title: World Heart Day 2026: the heart attack warning signs to know
dek: September 29 is World Heart Day. This year's "Don't Miss a Beat" campaign focuses on symptoms people overlook. Here are the signs and what to do.
keyPoints: Heart attack signs include chest pressure or pain, discomfort in the arms, back, neck, jaw or stomach, and shortness of breath.
Cold sweat, nausea, unusual fatigue and lightheadedness can also be signs, and women may notice vomiting or back, shoulder or arm pain.
The American Heart Association says to call 911 for any heart attack symptoms because minutes matter.
The World Heart Federation says 80% of cardiovascular deaths are linked to preventable or manageable risk factors.

sources.title: World Heart Federation launches 2026 Don't Miss a Beat campaign to highlight hidden symptoms of heart disease
Warning Signs of a Heart Attack | American Heart Association

body: Today is World Heart Day. The World Heart Federation's 2026 campaign is called "Don't Miss a Beat," and it focuses on the warning signs of heart disease that people often overlook or dismiss. The federation says cardiovascular disease claims more than 20 million lives each year, and that 80 percent of those deaths come from risk factors that can be prevented or managed.

So what are the signs? The American Heart Association lists chest discomfort that feels like pressure, squeezing, fullness or pain, lasting more than a few minutes or coming and going. Discomfort can also show up in one or both arms, the back, neck, jaw or stomach. Shortness of breath can happen with or without chest pain. Other signs include breaking out in a cold sweat, nausea, lightheadedness and unusual fatigue.

Symptoms are not always dramatic, and they can differ between men and women. The association notes that women may have signs less often linked with heart attacks, such as anxiety, vomiting, pain in the shoulder, back or arm, and unusual weakness. Its guidance is simple: call 911 if you have any symptoms of a heart attack, because minutes matter and emergency services are almost always the fastest way to get treatment.

The federation's campaign also offers an online "Are You Heart Smart?" quiz on myths, hidden symptoms and risk factors. This is general information, and a doctor is the right person to talk with about your own risk, blood pressure, cholesterol or any symptom that worries you.
Today, take a minute to read the warning signs with someone you live with, so both of you would know to call 911, and if a checkup is overdue, book it this week.
